books.section: Topic 7.7 1920s: Innovations in Communication and Technology

primary_sources: Photograph, “The Spirit of St. Louis, Col. Lindbergh's famous plane,” June 12, 1927

stimulus.text: The photograph, dated June 12, 1927, shows the airplane Spirit of St. Louis in a hangar, its name painted on the nose. Four men in work clothes and caps beside the plane — three standing, one crouching by the wheel — and a crowd stands behind them. A caption strip at the bottom reads: “The Spirit of St. Louis” — Col Lindbergh's famous plane. 6/12/27.
stimulus.source_note: Photograph, “The Spirit of St. Louis, Col. Lindbergh's famous plane,” June 12, 1927, National Photo Company Collection, Library of Congress LCCN92520351, public domain. Lindbergh himself does not appear in the photograph.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Library of Congress photograph, 1927, public domain
stem: Lindbergh's flight mattered most in the 1920s because it

options.text: made flying seem practical to the public
ended all government control of all aviation
options.misconception: The government kept regulating aviation after 1927. The flight changed public opinion, not the law.

options.text: proved that airplanes could not cross oceans
options.misconception: The flight proved the opposite: a single-engine plane did cross the ocean. That is why it mattered.

options.text: gave the United States a new air force
options.misconception: The flight did not create an air force. It changed how the public saw civilian flying.

rationales.A: Background: before 1927, most people saw flying as a stunt for daredevils. One solo crossing made the airplane look like practical transport, and airmail and passenger lines followed.
rationales.B: The government kept regulating aviation after 1927. The flight changed public opinion, not the law.
rationales.C: The flight proved the opposite: a single-engine plane did cross the ocean. That is why it mattered.
rationales.D: The flight did not create an air force. It changed how the public saw civilian flying.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what people thought of flying before 1927: a stunt for daredevils, not transport.
2. Ask what one solo crossing proved: a single-engine plane could cross an ocean.
3. Name the change: the public began to see the airplane as practical, and air travel grew.
Remember: a famous first matters when it changes what ordinary people believe is possible.
